tldr: By combining direct-drive (DD) motors with a low-ratio (1:2) differential transmission, the authors developed a 9-DOF, three-fingered robotic gripper that minimizes gearbox friction and inertia while achieving both practical grasping force (approx. 18 N) and exceptionally high physical transparency.
hero_caption: Appearance of the developed Differential Direct-Drive (DDD) gripper. A total of nine brushless DC motors are concentrated at the base of the three fingers (near the MCP joints), thoroughly lightweighting the distal links to achieve low inertia.
overview:
To interact dexterously with unknown environments and objects like humans do, a robot's end-effector needs "physical transparency" (backdrivability and low impedance to move compliantly in response to external forces), allowing it to sensitively feel contact forces and adapt instantly.

However, conventional robotic grippers rely on high-ratio transmissions to generate sufficient grasping torque. This introduces friction, backlash, and reflected inertia, severely degrading physical transparency. As a result, external force sensors become necessary to measure contact forces, which complicates the hardware and introduces delays into the control loop. Conversely, direct-drive (DD) designs without gear reducers offer superior transparency and responsiveness, but face a fundamental trade-off: standalone motor torque is small, making it difficult to deliver strong fingertip forces.

To tackle this, this study proposes a "Differential Direct-Drive (DDD)" mechanism that cleverly combines DD motors with a low-ratio (1:2) differential transmission. By centralizing all heavy actuators at the finger base, moving-link inertia is minimized, while a parallel two-motor drive doubles the torque during flexion.

Experiments on a physical 9-DOF, three-fingered prototype showed that while securing a nominal grasping force of approximately 18 N (fingertip force of 4.7 N), the unpowered passive mechanical impedance was at most 50.1 N/m, achieving an extremely compliant hand. Furthermore, closed-loop position control bandwidth reached 8.1 to 13.91 Hz. This provides human-level agility and establishes a foundation for high-precision sensorless force estimation from motor currents without external force sensors.
contributions: Proposed the Differential Direct-Drive (DDD) architecture fusing DD motors with a low-ratio (1:2) differential transmission, achieving both high torque and extreme physical transparency.

Concentrated motors at the finger base (MCP joint) while integrating counterweights, minimizing moving-link moments of inertia and limiting the motor contribution to total system inertia to just 0.236%.
Doubled torque during MCP flexion by operating two motors in parallel, achieving a 4.7 N fingertip force, 18 N grasping force, and approx. 2 kg payload despite using a direct-drive approach.
Experimentally demonstrated human-level high-speed response with closed-loop position control bandwidths of 8.1–13.91 Hz, alongside extremely low passive mechanical impedance of at most 50.1 N/m.

sections.heading: Why Do Conventional Grippers Fall Short? Tackling Physical Transparency
sections.summary: Dexterous manipulation in unstructured environments demands ultra-low inertia and high physical transparency to react instantly to contact forces. However, conventional high-ratio grippers degrade transparency due to friction and inertia. To overcome the torque limitations of direct drive (DD), this paper proposes the differential DDD gripper.
sections.details:
Dexterous manipulation inherently involves physical contact with cluttered, unknown environments. Adapting flexibly to these interactions requires hardware capable of reacting compliantly and inherently to contact forces—in other words, "ultra-low inertia" and "high physical transparency."

However, most conventional robotic grippers use high-ratio gearboxes to produce sufficient grasping torque. The trade-off is non-linear effects like gearbox friction, backlash, and reflected rotor inertia that scales with the square of the gear ratio, utterly destroying physical transparency. Because this distorts contact dynamics, many systems are forced to rely on external force sensors. Incorporating force sensors, however, complicates wiring and mechanical packaging while introducing dynamics and delays into the force control loop due to sensor filtering.

This has drawn attention to direct-drive (DD) motors, which eliminate reducers to provide exceptionally high backdrivability (the ability of the hand to be easily backdriven by external forces). With clean power transmission, DD systems achieve high control bandwidths and enable "sensorless force estimation" directly from motor currents. Yet without a reduction ratio, torque output remains inherently low. Quasi-direct-drive (QDD) actuators with low gear ratios have been explored, but they still fall short of pure DD transparency and struggle to provide sufficient degrees of freedom (DOF) for dexterous tasks.

To break the trade-offs among torque, physical transparency, and kinematic dexterity, this study proposes a 9-DOF, three-fingered Differential Direct-Drive (DDD) gripper combining DD motors with differential gearing. The goal is a dexterous hand capable of sensing external forces purely through motor currents without any external force sensors.

captions.F1: Overall configuration of the proposed DDD gripper. Three BLDC motors are placed at the base of each of the three fingers (nine motors total), clearly showing the structure that leaves moving distal links free of heavy actuators.

sections.heading: Differential Transmission Meets Direct Drive: The Secret to High Torque and Low Inertia
sections.summary: Three DD motors per finger are centralized at the base, utilizing a 1:2 differential transmission at the MCP joint (base) and a four-bar linkage at the IP joint. The differential mechanism sums (doubles) the torque of two motors during flexion, delivering sufficient grasping torque while preserving the benefits of direct drive.
sections.details:
The DDD gripper consists of three fingers, each powered by three DD motors, totaling nine motors across the hand. Each finger has two joints: the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint at the base and the interphalangeal (IP) joint toward the fingertip. In terms of degrees of freedom, each finger provides 3 DOFs: MCP flexion, MCP abduction/adduction, and IP flexion.

The core of this mechanism is the differential gear mechanism integrated into the MCP joint. As shown in Fig. F2, motion is determined by combining the rotational directions of two motors:
- Rotating the two motors synchronously in the same direction produces joint flexion (Co-DDD drive).
- Rotating the two motors in opposite directions produces joint abduction/adduction (Counter-DDD drive).
Meanwhile, the third motor placed further back drives IP joint flexion via a four-bar linkage. By restricting the linkage's operating range to its linear zone, singularities are avoided, achieving a 1:1 linear correspondence between motor angle and joint angle.

Why insert a differential gear rather than going with a pure DD setup? There are two primary reasons.

First is "ultra-low inertia through centralized mass." Centralizing all relatively heavy motor modules at the finger base minimizes the inertia of moving links being swept around, drastically boosting dynamic responsiveness.

Second is "efficient torque distribution." When grasping an object, the MCP joint requires much higher torque than the distal IP joint due to its longer moment arm. With a differential mechanism, the two motors work in parallel during MCP flexion, amplifying torque by 2x. Moreover, to minimize gear friction, the transmission ratio is kept extremely low at just 1:2. This preserves the inherent backdrivability and physical transparency of DD motors, solidifying the foundation for high-bandwidth control and sensorless force estimation.

captions.F2: Operating principle of the DDD mechanism. Rotating two motors in the same direction doubles torque for MCP flexion (left), while opposite rotation drives abduction/adduction (center). The IP joint is driven independently by a DD motor via a four-bar linkage (right).

sections.heading: Prototype and Evaluation: Ultra-Low Impedance and High Bandwidth
sections.summary: The authors fabricated a 2.4 kg prototype using 3D printing and compact BLDC motors. While achieving an 18 N grasping force and a 2 kg payload, passive mechanical impedance remained below 50.1 N/m, the motor contribution to total inertia was kept to just 0.236%, and closed-loop bandwidth reached 8.1–13.91 Hz, surpassing human capability.
sections.details:
The developed prototype uses compact BLDC motors from CubeMars (GL35) as actuators, and the frame structure was fabricated using a Formlabs stereolithography 3D printer (Form 4). A single finger module weighs approximately 800 g, bringing the entire three-fingered gripper to 2.4 kg. Placing DD motors near the MCP joint shifts the center of mass, so integrated counterweights kinematically optimize the mass distribution. This eases the burden of gravity compensation and helps maintain balance even during high-speed motions.

Physical evaluation yielded impressive metrics:
- Output torque and grasping force: Each module delivers 4.7 N of fingertip force, yielding a nominal three-fingered grasping force of approx. 18 N and the ability to grasp payloads of about 2 kg.
- Ultra-low inertia: The motor contribution to the total system inertia is suppressed to just 0.236%. Thanks to the minimal gear ratio, reflected rotor inertia has almost zero impact.
- Passive mechanical impedance: The authors measured mechanical stiffness ($|F/x|$) against external forces with motors completely unpowered. Even the stiffest MCP abduction/adduction axis was only 50.1 N/m, the MCP flexion axis was 15.6 N/m, and the PIP (IP) flexion axis was merely 9.5 N/m. These numbers confirm an extraordinarily compliant hand where fingertips yield smoothly to external forces.

Furthermore, to verify whether the system could move with human-level agility, closed-loop position frequency responses were measured using chirp signal inputs (0.1 to 30 Hz). As shown in Fig. F3, the $-3\text{ dB}$ bandwidths were:
- MCP flexion: $8.10\text{ Hz}$
- MCP abduction/adduction: $11.38\text{ Hz}$ (indicated as $11.39\text{ Hz}$ in the plot)
- PIP flexion: $13.91\text{ Hz}$

Because both motors rotate in the same direction during MCP flexion, equivalent rotational inertia is maximized and response is slowest, yet it still exceeds 8 Hz. Meanwhile, the fully direct-driven PIP flexion demonstrated an agile, high-speed response exceeding 13.9 Hz.

captions.F3: Closed-loop position control frequency responses (Bode plots) for each joint. The $-3\text{ dB}$ bandwidth reached 8.10 Hz for MCP flexion, 11.39 Hz for abduction/adduction, and 13.91 Hz for PIP flexion, demonstrating high responsiveness surpassing human levels.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Next Steps: Paving the Way for Sensorless Dexterous Manipulation
sections.summary: The proposed DDD gripper successfully resolves the trade-off among torque, physical transparency, and dexterity. Moving forward, the team aims to leverage this extreme transparency and low inertia to achieve advanced sensorless manipulation, estimating and controlling contact forces using only motor currents and dynamic models without force sensors.
sections.details:
This study developed a novel 9-DOF Differential Direct-Drive (DDD) gripper that resolves the trade-offs among torque output, physical transparency, and kinematic dexterity. By pairing DD motors with a modest 1:2 differential transmission, the design secures practical grasping force (nominal 18 N) while achieving ultra-low inertia. These hardware characteristics strongly indicate that high-bandwidth force control and robust environmental interaction are achievable without relying on external force sensors.

Looking ahead, the authors' primary focus is establishing a proprioceptive force estimation framework. Because the mechanism's friction and inertia are pushed to absolute minimums and backdrivability is high, combining motor current commands with an accurate dynamic model should enable sensorless, high-precision estimation of external forces applied to fingertips.

Future plans include refining the mechanical structure through lightweighting and stiffness optimization, moving toward the demonstration of advanced sensorless dexterous manipulation that can adapt flexibly and safely in unstructured environments.

takeaways: The "DD motor + 1:2 differential transmission" approach is a clever design solution that doubles required grasping torque without sacrificing any of direct drive's extreme transparency or high responsiveness.

Centralizing actuators at the base restricts the motor inertia contribution to 0.236%, achieving an unpowered passive impedance of at most 50.1 N/m for an end-effector that yields remarkably smoothly to external forces.

With closed-loop position bandwidths of 8–14 Hz, the system promises fast adaptive control on par with or exceeding human capability during dynamic manipulation and collisions with unknown environments.
This architecture serves as an ideal hardware benchmark for researchers seeking "sensorless force control"—estimating contact forces directly from motor currents instead of external force sensors.
limitations: With a nominal grasping force of approx. 18 N, fingertip force of 4.7 N, and payload of approx. 2 kg, torque may be insufficient for heavy-load, heavy-duty industrial handling.
The MCP flexion frequency response (8.10 Hz) is noticeably lower than PIP flexion (13.91 Hz), as the increased equivalent inertia from differential actuation acts as a bottleneck on response speed.
This paper is currently limited to hardware design and fundamental impedance/frequency response validation; sensorless force estimation and actual dexterous manipulation tasks remain future work.
